analysis.one_liner: Requires brand-name drug makers to sell samples to generic developers so cheaper copies can reach the market.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a House committee and its Health Subcommittee in September 2014 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drug companies sometimes refuse to sell samples of their own drugs to companies trying to develop generics or biosimilars, which blocks the testing needed for FDA approval and keeps monopoly prices in place after patents expire. This bill would have made it illegal for brand-name makers to restrict that access, including through FDA safety programs, and would have let the FTC and private companies sue violators for triple damages. It died in committee without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who pay for prescription drugs, because faster generic and biosimilar competition lowers prices. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers, who would gain guaranteed access to the reference drugs they need for testing.

how_it_helps.text: The bill's findings state that brand-name license holders restrict access to their drugs by companies developing generics and biosimilars, which deters and delays cheaper competition and extends patent monopolies beyond their lawful life [S3].

It would have required the FDA to prohibit license holders from restricting supply of approved drugs to product developers, including restrictions imposed through risk evaluation and mitigation strategies (REMS), the FDA safety programs that brand makers used to refuse samples [S2].

It would have set up an FDA authorization process with a 60-day deadline so developers could obtain reasonable quantities of a drug at market-based prices, even directly from the brand maker if wholesalers would not sell [S3].

It would have let authorized developers sue license holders for injunctive relief and treble damages, and required the FDA and FTC to report annually to Congress on noncompliance and its effect on market entry and prices [S2].

It would have allowed a generic applicant to waive the single, shared REMS safety system requirement if it tried in good faith for 120 days to negotiate entry and the brand maker refused commercially reasonable terms [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would lose a tool for delaying generic and biosimilar entry and the extended monopoly revenue that comes with it, plus the new liability for antitrust-style treble damages suits.

drawbacks.text: The bill grants brand-name license holders immunity from any claim arising out of a generic developer's testing activities, even a claim arising from the developer's failure to follow adequate safeguards for safe use, shifting risk away from the brand maker during testing [S3].

It overrides distribution restrictions imposed through REMS, FDA's safety programs for high-risk drugs such as those with serious side effects, relying on the FDA to verify that a developer's testing protocol offers comparable safety protections — a judgment regulators would have to police case by case [S2].

By weakening one lever brands used to slow competition, it would speed entry of generic and biosimilar competitors, which the bill's supporters intended but which reduces revenue that funds brand-drug research, a trade-off an honest supporter would acknowledge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core mechanism targets a documented anti-competitive practice: blocking sample access to stall generic approval. The consumer payoff — faster generic and biosimilar entry and lower prices — outweighs the costs, though the liability immunity for brand makers during testing is a genuine concession and the FDA would carry a new policing burden on safety protocols.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then its Health Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Stivers (R-OH) introduced the bill on September 18, 2014, joined by Rep. Peter Welch (D-VT) [S1].
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and the next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health [S5].
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — was taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers, which kept the ability to restrict competitors' access to samples of their drugs and thereby delay cheaper generic and biosimilar competition, preserving extended monopoly pricing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican sponsor and a Democratic cosponsor, and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan opposition ever appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped brands of their ability to refuse sample access to generic and biosimilar developers, including through REMS safety programs, ending a practice the bill's findings describe as extending patent monopolies beyond their lawful life. Their loss — extended monopoly pricing — came directly at consumers' expense.

The bill guaranteed them access to reference products at market-based prices and a waiver from the shared REMS system if negotiations failed, letting them bring cheaper competition to market faster. Their interest runs alongside consumers' interests in lower drug prices.

The bill would have required them to fill anonymous sample requests at market-based prices and barred them from disclosing the developer's identity to the brand maker. They would be paid market rates but would carry new obligations.
